title: Frontier pre-training at Microsoft AI (MAI-Base-2 report)
why: The document the whole deck follows: MAI-Base-2's architecture, the scaling ladders, hyperparameter laws, MoE and Muon systems work, clipping, and the data mixture; Figures 1-10 are reproduced from it. Not on arXiv; the PDF was supplied for the lecture.

title: PaLM: scaling language modeling with Pathways
why: Defines model FLOPs utilization (MFU), the 21% figure the report quotes; Section 5.1 also describes restarting around loss spikes, the practice MAI-Base-2 avoided.

title: Language modeling is compression
why: Why a language model's log-loss is a compression rate: the arithmetic-coding argument behind reading bits per byte as a compression score.

title: Outrageously large neural networks: the sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layer
why: Sparse top-k gating at scale: a learned router makes a layer's cost independent of its parameter count, and introduces the load-balancing losses later work inherits.

title: GShard: scaling giant models with conditional computation and automatic sharding
why: Top-2 MoE in transformers at 600B parameters; expert parallelism, capacity factors and token dropping as used since.

title: Switch Transformers: scaling to trillion parameter models with simple and efficient sparsity
why: Top-1 routing, the auxiliary load-balancing loss with its 0.01 weight, and the first trillion-parameter sparse model.

title: DeepSeekMoE: towards ultimate expert specialization in mixture-of-experts language models
why: Fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts, the design MAI-Base-2's 1 shared + 7 of 512 layout follows.

title: GQA: training generalized multi-query transformer models from multi-head checkpoints
why: Grouped-query attention: query heads share key/value heads, shrinking the KV cache by the group size; MAI-Base-2 uses 48 queries per KV head in global layers and 6 in local ones.

title: Using the output embedding to improve language models
why: Tied input and output embeddings, the default MAI-Base-1 used and MAI-Base-2 abandoned.

title: Scaling laws for neural language models
why: Power laws in parameters, data and compute over seven orders of magnitude, and the 6ND cost model behind every FLOPs number in the deck.

title: Training compute-optimal large language models
why: Chinchilla: the parametric fit L = E + A/N^a + B/D^b and the roughly 20 tokens-per-parameter optimum that MAI-Base-2's 625 TPP sits far beyond.

title: Resolving discrepancies in compute-optimal scaling of language models
why: Why Kaplan and Chinchilla disagreed: embedding parameters, warmup and learning-rate tuning at small scale; a warning about what a ladder must control.

title: Scaling data-constrained language models
why: Repeating data up to about four epochs is nearly free, then returns decay; the regime that source scaling reproduces on every rung.

title: Establishing task scaling laws via compute-efficient model ladders
why: The ladder method made explicit: a family of small models with one recipe predicts the large model's task performance within a few points.

title: A hitchhiker's guide to scaling law estimation
why: How to fit and extrapolate laws in practice: how many models, which sizes, intermediate checkpoints, and the usual errors.

title: Decoupled weight decay regularization
why: AdamW: weight decay applied as a multiplicative shrink (1 - lr*wd) rather than as an L2 term in the gradient, which is why the product lr*wd is the quantity that matters.

title: How to set AdamW's weight decay as you scale model and dataset size
why: The EMA view of AdamW with timescale 1/(lr*wd), and the argument that the timescale should be a fixed fraction of training; the report's exponent of -1 is this rule.

title: On the SDEs and scaling rules for adaptive gradient algorithms
why: Derives the square-root scaling rule for Adam-type optimizers: double the batch, multiply the learning rate by sqrt(2); the report's exponent of -0.5 in steps.

title: Tensor Programs V: tuning large neural networks via zero-shot hyperparameter transfer
why: muP: parameterize so the optimal learning rate does not move with width; the alternative to fitting empirical hyperparameter laws.

title: DeepSeek LLM: scaling open-source language models with longtermism
why: Empirical scaling laws for learning rate and batch size against compute, fitted the same way as the report's laws for LR and weight decay.

title: MiniCPM: unveiling the potential of small language models with scalable training strategies
why: Warmup-stable-decay schedules and muP in a practical small-model ladder; how hyperparameter sweeps are made affordable.

title: Dropout: a simple way to prevent neural networks from overfitting
why: The regularizer whose rate the report sets by a scaling law in active parameters. JMLR 15. Not on arXiv.

title: MegaBlocks: efficient sparse training with mixture-of-experts
why: Dropless MoE with block-sparse kernels: no token dropping, but memory that moves with the routing; the design MAI's fixed-memory multi-round scheme improves on.

title: DeepSpeed-MoE: advancing mixture-of-experts inference and training to power next-generation AI scale
why: Expert parallelism at scale in a production training stack, with the communication and memory bookkeeping that per-expert overhead comes from.

title: Tutel: adaptive mixture-of-experts at scale
why: Adaptive parallelism and pipelining for MoE layers, including dynamic capacity factors; the systems background for dispatch/collect scheduling.

title: ST-MoE: designing stable and transferable sparse expert models
why: The router z-loss and a careful study of MoE training stability; how capacity factor and token dropping affect quality.

title: Auxiliary-loss-free load balancing strategy for mixture-of-experts
why: Balancing expert load with a per-expert bias instead of a loss term; the alternative to the batched load-balancing loss the report describes.

title: Reducing activation recomputation in large transformer models
why: Activation recomputation (rematerialization) and how to minimize it; the compute that memory freed from MoE buffers buys back.

title: Muon: an optimizer for hidden layers in neural networks
why: The origin of Muon: orthogonalize the momentum of each weight matrix with five bfloat16 Newton-Schulz iterations. Blog post; not on arXiv.

title: Old optimizer, new norm: an anthology
why: Muon as steepest descent under the spectral norm; why equalizing singular values of the update is the natural step for a matrix parameter.

title: Muon is scalable for LLM training
why: Weight decay and update-scale adjustments that make Muon work at scale; about twice AdamW's compute efficiency on a 16B MoE.

title: Kimi K2: open agentic intelligence
why: A 1T-parameter MoE trained with MuonClip over 15.5T tokens with no loss spikes; the largest public Muon run before MAI-Base-2.

title: ZeRO: memory optimizations toward training trillion parameter models
why: Sharding optimizer state across data-parallel GPUs, which is why Muon's momentum has to be resharded before Newton-Schulz.

title: Fantastic pretraining optimizers and where to find them
why: A controlled comparison of Muon, SOAP, Shampoo and AdamW across scales; how much of the gain survives careful tuning.

title: FP8 formats for deep learning
why: E4M3 and E5M2: the two 8-bit floats, their ranges, and tensor-wise scaling with a delayed scale, MAI-Base-1's scheme.

title: Microscaling data formats for deep learning
why: MX formats: blocks of 32 values sharing an 8-bit power-of-two scale; MXFP8 is MAI-Base-2's training format.

title: Recipes for pre-training LLMs with MXFP8
why: How to train with MXFP8 in practice: scale rounding, which tensors to quantize, and matching BF16 on an 8B model over 15T tokens.

title: Scaling FP8 training to trillion-token LLMs
why: FP8 instabilities that appear only after hundreds of billions of tokens, and their fix; why a stable FP8 recipe must be tested at full horizon.

title: On the difficulty of training recurrent neural networks
why: Global-norm gradient clipping, the standard guard that MAI-Base-1 used alone and MAI-Base-2 supplements with activation gradient clipping.

title: Scaling vision transformers to 22 billion parameters
why: Attention-logit growth as a cause of divergence and QK-normalization as the fix; the canonical example of a stability fix found by looking inside the network.

title: Small-scale proxies for large-scale transformer training instabilities
why: Reproduces loss spikes at small scale by raising the learning rate; QK-norm, z-loss and the LR sensitivity of large models; what a ladder can and cannot reveal about stability.

title: 2 OLMo 2 furious
why: A fully open run that documents its stability fixes (initialization, normalization, z-loss) and its gradient-norm traces; a public counterpart to Figures 5 and 7.

title: The FineWeb datasets: decanting the web for the finest text data at scale
why: A documented web-data pipeline (parse, filter, dedup, classify) with ablations for each stage; the open counterpart to MAI's in-house pipeline.

title: DataComp-LM: in search of the next generation of training sets for language models
why: A benchmark for data curation at fixed compute; quality classifiers give the largest gains, as the report also finds.

title: SemDeDup: data-efficient learning at web-scale through semantic deduplication
why: Embedding-based removal of near-duplicates that exact matching misses; the technique behind diversity sampling.

title: D4: improving LLM pretraining via document de-duplication and diversification
why: Picks a diverse subset in embedding space and beats random selection at equal tokens; the closest published analogue of the report's diversity sampling.

title: Data mixing laws: optimizing data mixtures by predicting language modeling performance
why: Loss as a function of domain proportions, fitted on small runs to choose the mix for a large one; how a Figure 10 mixture can be chosen rather than guessed.

title: An image is worth 16x16 words: transformers for image recognition at scale
why: Images as sequences of linearly embedded patches; the patch embedding that an encoder-free VLM feeds straight into the language model.

title: Fuyu-8B: a multimodal architecture for AI agents
why: The first widely used encoder-free VLM: image patches projected linearly into a decoder-only transformer, any resolution. Blog post; not on arXiv.

title: Unveiling encoder-free vision-language models
why: A systematic study of removing the vision encoder: what data and training it takes for a pure decoder to match encoder-based VLMs.

title: PaliGemma: a versatile 3B VLM for transfer
why: The encoder-plus-projector design the slide contrasts with MAI's, done carefully; useful for seeing exactly what the encoder-free route gives up and gains.

title: DeepSeek-V3 technical report
why: The reference open frontier recipe: 671B/37B MoE with 1 shared + 8 of 256 experts, block-scaled FP8 training, and multi-token prediction; the design MAI-Base-2's MoE layout is closest to.

title: Qwen3 technical report
why: The lineage of the Qwen3.8 comparator: fine-grained MoE, GQA, and a documented pre-training mixture of 36T tokens.

title: Gated Delta Networks: improving Mamba2 with delta rule
why: The linear-attention layer (Gated DeltaNet) that Qwen3.8 interleaves 3:1 with full attention, per its model card.

title: Kimi Linear: an expressive, efficient attention architecture
why: Kimi Delta Attention, the linear layer Kimi K3 mixes with gated MLA, per its model card.

title: The Llama 4 herd: the beginning of a new era of natively multimodal AI innovation
why: Natively multimodal MoE models with interleaved local and global attention (iRoPE); a contemporary of the MAI design. Blog post; not on arXiv.

title: DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base model card (Hugging Face)
why: Source of the comparator row on slide 5b: 1.6T total / 49B active, 61 layers, compressed sparse attention, base weights trained on more than 32T tokens. Model card; secondary source.

title: Kimi-K3 model card (Hugging Face)
why: Source of the comparator row on slide 5b: 2.8T / 104B, 93 layers, 896 experts with 16 active and 2 shared, 69 Kimi Delta Attention + 24 gated MLA layers, MXFP4 weights. Model card; secondary source.

title: Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B model card (Hugging Face)
why: Source of the comparator row on slide 5b: 2.4T / 95B, 92 layers, 512 experts with 10 active and 1 shared, 69 Gated DeltaNet + 23 attention layers. Model card; secondary source.

title: MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL model card (Hugging Face)
why: Source of the comparator row on slide 5b: 1.02T / 42B, 70 layers, 384 experts with 8 active, sliding-window plus global attention. Model card; secondary source.
